questions.question_text: Physiological changes in pregnancy affecting drug metabolism
questions.explanation: In pregnancy, GFR increases and renal elimination increases. Only absorption, protein binding, and gastric emptying (APE) typically decrease; other parameters related to metabolism remain relatively unaffected.

questions.question_text: What prenatal effect is attributed to maternal depression?

options.text: Higher preterm birth and low birth weight

correct_answer.text: Higher preterm birth and low birth weight

questions.explanation: The source explicitly lists poor nutrition, higher preterm birth, low birth weight, and pre-eclampsia as prenatal effects of maternal depression.

questions.question_text: Maria suffered from postpartum blues during the immediate postpartum period, what is the chance that she develops postpartum depression?
questions.explanation: The most common constellation of mood symptoms experienced by women in the immediate postpartum period is typically referred to as the postpartum blues or baby blues. A relatively common phenomenon (occurring in 50–80% of women), postpartum blues include transient symptoms and rapid mood shifts, including tearfulness, irritability, anxiety, insomnia, lack of energy, loss of appetite, and the general experience of feeling overwhelmed particularly with regard to newborn care-giving tasks. By defi nition, the postpartum blues are transient in nature. Onset typically occurs after the third postpartum day, after the mother has left the hospital after delivery. Symptoms typically peak by day 5 and spontaneously resolve by day 10 postpartum. It has been estimated that 75% of women who experience symptoms of postpartum blues will display such a time-limited course; however, 20–25% may go on to experience full-blown postpartum depression. Kaplan HI. Kaplan and Sadock’s Comprehensive Textbook of Psychiatry, 8th edn. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2004 p. 2308.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is increased in pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Pregnancy is associated with decreased gastric acid production, leading to increased gastric pH. Additionally, glomerular filtration rate is increased in pregnancy. Gastric emptying and intestinal motility decrease, plasma protein binding decreases due to reduced albumin, and volume of distribution increases.

questions.question_text: Which physiological change occurs in pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Pregnancy causes an increase in glomerular filtration rate (GFR), which is one of the most significant physiological changes affecting drug metabolism and renal function.

questions.question_text: Psychosis with peripartum onset is MOST closely related to which class of psychiatric disorders?
questions.explanation: Evidence suggests a relationship between psychosis with peripartum onset and mood disorders, including bipolar disorder and major depressive disorder. Re FeRe NCe Sadock, B. J., & Sadock, V. A. (2003). Other psychotic disorders. In Kaplan and Sadock’s synopsis of psychiatry (9th ed., p. 526). Philadelphia, PA: Lippincott Williams and Wilkins.

questions.explanation: Lithium is a firstline agent for the management of bipolar disorder in pregnancy despite concerns for increased risk of 282 • PsyChiatRy Ebstein’s anomaly. The absolute risk of Ebstein’s anomaly is 1 to 2/ 1,000 in firsttrimester exposure as compared with 1/ 20,000 in the general population.

questions.question_text: Which of the following medications increases the risk of autism when used during pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Sodium valproate (valproic acid) exposure during pregnancy has been associated with an increased risk of autism spectrum disorder in exposed offspring, as demonstrated in multiple epidemiological studies.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which is the best screening tool used in post-natal depression?

options.text: A diagnosis of edinburgh postnatal depression scale
A diagnosis of beck’s depression inventory

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of edinburgh postnatal depression scale

questions.explanation: Common somatic complaints of pregnancy may be misconstrued as symptoms of depression when using traditional depression assessment scales (such as the Beck Depression Inventory, the Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression, or the Center for Epidemiological Studies Depression Scale), symptoms of depression reported by pregnant women may be misidentifi ed as normal pregnancy-related complaints by treating obstetricians. Use of the 10-item Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale has been found to accurately identify depression in pregnant and postpartum women. This brief screening instrument has been validated in pregnant and postpartum populations and is easily incorporated for standard practice use in obstetrical treatment settings. Kaplan HI. Kaplan and Sadock’s Comprehensive Textbook of Psychiatry, 8th edn. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2004 p. 2306.

questions.question_text: What is a recognized complication of paroxetine use in late pregnancy?
questions.explanation: SSRI use in late pregnancy, particularly paroxetine, is associated with persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) and neonatal adaptation syndrome.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman taking sodium valproate is counseled regarding teratogenic risks. Which of the following is a recognized congenital malformation associated with prenatal valproate exposure?

options.text: Cleft palate and cardiac defects only
Bilateral aplasia of the radius and developmental delay only
Congenital malformations including facial dysmorphism, cleft lip/palate, cardiac, renal, urogenital defects, limb defects, and developmental delays

correct_answer.text: Congenital malformations including facial dysmorphism, cleft lip/palate, cardiac, renal, urogenital defects, limb defects, and developmental delays

questions.explanation: Sodium valproate is associated with congenital malformations occurring in 8-12% of exposed pregnancies, including facial dysmorphism, cleft lip and palate, craniostenosis, cardiac, renal and urogenital defects, and limb defects (including bilateral aplasia of the radius). Developmental delays occur in 31-40% of exposed children. Valproate is contraindicated in pregnancy.

questions.question_text: Prenatal exposure to alcohol is most commonly linked to development of which of the following psychiatric disorders?

options.text: A diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder
A diagnosis of intellectual disability disorder
A diagnosis of major depressive disorder

questions.explanation: Psychiatric conditions are common in individuals with histories of significant prenatal exposure to alcohol. The most predominant psychiatric diagnosis is ADHD. Oppositional defiant disorder and conduct disorder are also quite common. The presence of mood disorders has been described, including depression and bipolar disorder. Prenatal exposure to alcohol is a risk factor for subsequent development of tobacco, alcohol, and other substance use disorders. Re FeRe NCe American Psychiatric Association. (2013). Diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders (5th ed., pp. 800– 801). Arlington, VA: American Psychiatric Publishing.

questions.explanation: According to NIDA data cited in Kaplan & Sadock\'s Synopsis of Psychiatry (p.2317), approximately 19% of pregnant women report alcohol use during pregnancy, which is approximately 1 in 5

questions.question_text: Which statement is true regarding clozapine use in pregnancy?

options.text: Dose needs to be increased due to enzyme induction
Dose needs to be increased due to increased GFR
Dose reduction is required due to enzyme inhibition by estrogens
It has no effects on the fetus

correct_answer.text: Dose reduction is required due to enzyme inhibition by estrogens

questions.explanation: During pregnancy, estrogens inhibit CYP1A2 (clozapine's main metabolic enzyme), reducing clozapine metabolism and increasing plasma levels; dose reduction may be necessary.

questions.question_text: Why does lithium plasma level decrease during pregnancy?
questions.explanation: During pregnancy, maternal physiological changes include increased plasma volume and increased renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate (GFR increases by 50%). This enhanced renal clearance leads to decreased plasma levels of lithium and other renally eliminated drugs.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman with mania requires emergency restraint and rapid tranquilization in an inpatient unit. What is the most appropriate course of action following the incident?

options.text: Reduce benzodiazepine and antipsychotic doses by 50%
Apply restraint as you would if she were not pregnant

correct_answer.text: Apply restraint as you would if she were not pregnant

questions.explanation: Restraint should be applied using same principles; pregnancy doesn't change restraint technique.

questions.question_text: Donna is an active opiate user, who recently found out that she is pregnant. She approaches her GP saying she wants to stop her substance use and is not considering maintenance treatment with methadone. She is worried about withdrawal symptoms. Her GP calls you about the best time for Donna to undergo opiate withdrawal during pregnancy. Which of the following is the most appropriate answer?

options.text: Withdrawal should be avoided in all trimesters due to fetal risk
Maintenance methadone is contraindicated in pregnancy

questions.explanation: The view of treatment of opiate dependence has changed over the past 25 years. Previously it was thought that all patients should undergo withdrawal prior to delivery. Current practice acknowledges the fact that an abstinence state is almost impossible to achieve in this population. Hence most experts now advocate methadone maintenance as a way to reduce illegal drug use and remove the woman from a hazardous drug-seeking environment. Current consensus is that undertaking a medical withdrawal regimen could be accomplished most safely during the second trimester, with careful monitoring of foetal welfare by perinatal experts. The consensus is that opiate withdrawal could be best accomplished through stabilization with methadone followed by gradual reduction of the methadone dosage by 2–2.5 mg every 7–10 days. This should ideally be done only in a secondary care setting with the involvement of obstetricians and neonatologists. Lowinson JH, Ruiz P, Millman RB and Langrod JG. Substance Abuse: A Comprehensive Textbook, 4th edn. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2005, p. 808.

questions.question_text: Which statement most accurately characterizes postpartum hypomania?

options.text: It characteristically emerges during the third trimester of pregnancy.
It occurs in approximately 5-10% of postpartum women.
It is a risk factor for postpartum depression.
It is indistinguishable from normal maternal mood fluctuations in most cases.
It is more common in nulliparous women.

correct_answer.text: It is a risk factor for postpartum depression.

questions.explanation: Childbirth may be a specific trigger for a hypomanic episode, which can occur in 10%–20% of females in nonclinical populations and most typically in the early postpartum period. Distinguishing hypomania from the elated mood and reduced sleep that normally accompany the birth of a child may be challenging. Postpartum hypomania may foreshadow the onset of a depression that occurs in about half of females who experience postpartum “highs.” Accurate detection of bipolar II disorder may help in establishing appropriate treatment of the depression, which may reduce the risk of suicide and infanticide.

questions.explanation: Pregnancy is associated with a decrease in production of gastric acid, leading to an increase in overall gastric pH.

questions.explanation: Depression during pregnancy – 7 to 15% risk (around 10%) and notes that this is higher than the 7% rate in non-perinatal women. While 10% is mentioned as around, the question asks for the stated prevalence estimate, and 7% is given as the lower bound of the range. questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that drugs account for only 5 of every 100 malformations that occur in pregnancy. questions.question_text: A newborn baby is observed to be jittery, shaking, and tachypnoeic. Which of the following drugs taken by the mother is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Stimulant use, particularly cocaine, prior to delivery is associated with neonatal withdrawal syndrome including symptoms of agitation, jitteriness, shaking, vomiting, and tachypnea. These symptoms typically appear within the first few hours after birth. Cocaine crosses the placental barrier and causes sympathomimetic effects in the newborn, presenting with hyperactivity, tremors, and elevated vital signs.

correct_answer.text: Low birth weight and preterm birth

questions.explanation: The source explicitly lists prenatal effects of maternal depression as poor nutrition, higher preterm birth, low birth weight, pre-eclampsia. Options A, C, D, and E are not mentioned as consequences of maternal depression in the provided text.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman with bipolar I disorder is scheduled for induction of labour next week. Her lithium dose has been increased in recent weeks, and she has a current level of 0.75 mmol/L. She is not planning to breastfeed. What is the most advisable course of management?

options.text: Suspend lithium 24-48 hours before induction and re-check the level 12 hours after the last dose
Reduce the lithium dose to 400 mg and re-check the level 1 week post-delivery
Maintain current lithium dosing and re-check the level 4 weeks post-delivery
Check the lithium level daily until her induction, then discontinue lithium until 4 weeks post-delivery
As she is not planning to breastfeed, no changes in lithium dosing or further bloodwork are advised

correct_answer.text: Suspend lithium 24-48 hours before induction and re-check the level 12 hours after the last dose

questions.explanation: In the third trimester, lithium requirements increase due to increased total body water, but these requirements return abruptly to pre-pregnancy levels immediately after delivery, risking maternal and neonatal intoxication. Lithium should be suspended for 24-48 hours before planned induction or Caesarean section and at onset of labour. Lithium levels should be measured 12 hours after the last dose. If levels are not above therapeutic range, lithium should be restarted on day 1 postnatal and checked again after 1 week.

options.text: Neonatal withdrawal syndrome and floppy infant syndrome

questions.question_text: Mental health problems are identified in more than 90% of individuals with a history of significant prenatal alcohol exposure. Which of the following is the MOST common co-occurring psychiatric diagnosis in this group?
questions.explanation:
Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is the most common co-occurring psychiatric diagnosis in individuals with significant prenatal alcohol exposure / fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD)
.

Environmental Driver: Prenatal exposure to alcohol is a well-established environmental risk factor for the development of ADHD and executive dysfunction
.
Core Behavioral & Neurocognitive Profile: Individuals with FASD present with marked neurocognitive deficits that heavily overlap with ADHD, including hyperactivity, impulsivity, poor impulse control, inattention, visuospatial difficulties, and memory deficits

Associated Features: FASD frequently co-occurs with mild learning disabilities (intellectual disability) as well as speech and language impairments

questions.question_text: Compared with the general population, the risk of Ebstein’s anomaly in children of mothers exposed to lithium during the fi rst trimester of pregnancy is
questions.explanation: The risk of major congenital anomalies in children exposed to lithium in the uterus is 4–12%. This is nearly three times higher than non-exposed fetuses. The UK National Teratology Information Service has concluded that lithium increases the risk of cardiac malformations by approximately eightfold. First trimester exposure to lithium increases the risk of Ebstein’s anomaly by nearly 10–20 times, bringing the absolute risk to 0.05–0.1%. Stein G and Wilkinson G, eds. questions.question_text: Which screening tool is most appropriate for postpartum depression?
questions.explanation: The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) is the gold standard screening tool for postpartum depression and is widely used in clinical practice.

questions.question_text: A newborn presents with microcephaly, challenging behaviour, and poor memory with a birth weight of 2kg. Which maternal substance exposure is most likely?
questions.explanation: Fetal alcohol syndrome is characterized by microcephaly, intrauterine growth restriction (low birth weight), neurodevelopmental problems, and behavioral difficulties.

questions.question_text: What is the approximate percentage of children exposed to sodium valproate monotherapy during pregnancy who develop congenital malformations?
questions.explanation: Approximately 10% of children exposed to valproate monotherapy during pregnancy suffer from congenital malformations (compared to the general population risk of 2-3%). The risk is dose-dependent. Valproate exposure is also associated with increased risk of autism spectrum disorder.

questions.question_text: If carbamazepine and phenytoin are administered together during pregnancy, which fetal malformation would be expected?
questions.explanation: The combination of carbamazepine and phenytoin (both aromatic antiepileptic drugs) during pregnancy is associated with fetal anticonvulsant syndrome, which can include finger nail hypoplasia among other features including cleft palate and cardiac abnormalities.

questions.question_text: Which screening tool is used to identify postnatal depression?
questions.explanation: The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) is a 10-item self-report questionnaire specifically designed to screen for postnatal depression in the postpartum period. It has good sensitivity and specificity for identifying postpartum depression.

questions.question_text: What is the risk of congenital malformations with maternal valproate exposure?
questions.explanation: Maternal valproate exposure carries a congenital anomaly risk of 8-12%, along with developmental delays occurring in 31-40% of exposed children.

questions.question_text: What Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) score is suggestive of caseness (likely depression)?
questions.explanation: An EPDS score of 12-13 or above is considered suggestive of caseness and indicates probable postnatal depression requiring further assessment and intervention.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the strongest predictor of developing depressive symptoms during pregnancy?

options.text: A diagnosis of paranoid personality disorder

questions.explanation: A previous history of depression is the strongest predictor of depressive symptoms during pregnancy and of postnatal depression; perinatal psychiatric risk assessment therefore centres on past psychiatric history. Socioeconomic disadvantage, being unmarried/lacking partner support and minority ethnic status are recognised but comparatively weaker contextual risk factors, often mediated through stress and reduced social support. Paranoid personality disorder is not an established predictor of antenatal depression.

questions.question_text: A 25yearold female, G2P2, who is 10 days postpartum comes to the emergency room with severe leftsided headache with blurred vision. While in the emergency room, she has a general tonic–c lonic seizure. Initial head CT scan shows no acute findings, but MR venogram shows absent flow in the right transverse sinus, sigmoid sinus, and internal jugular vein. What is the appropriate treatment for this condition? t OF NEUROLOGICAL DISORDERS • 167
questions.explanation: Cerebral venous thrombosis is frequently missed and misdiagnosed because it is considered to be a rare clinical entity. It has been associated with hypercoagulable states as in pregnancy or postpartum or with the use of oral contraceptives. Although variable in presentation, it commonly presents with severe headaches, delirium, and seizures. Laboratory tests, including coagulation labs, can be useful, but definite diagnosis requires neuroimaging. Head CT scan can be normal in up to 30% of cases. MRI in conjunction with MR venography is highly sensitive and specific for this diagnosis. Treatment includes use of anticoagulants based on current guidelines. Mannitol can be useful for the management of intracranial pressure as needed. Valproate can be used for seizure prophylaxis.

questions.question_text: Which is an appropriate screening tool for postnatal depression?
questions.explanation: The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) is a validated screening tool specifically designed for postnatal depression.

questions.question_text: The risk of congenital anomalies associated with valproate exposure during pregnancy is approximately:
questions.explanation: Valproate exposure during pregnancy carries a risk of congenital anomalies of 8-12%, along with developmental delays occurring in 31-40% of exposed infants.

questions.question_text: When treating pregnant women with mental health difficulties, the benefits of medications must be carefully balanced against the potential risks involved. Which of the following medications is felt to be most risky for a developing foetus?
questions.explanation: Valproate can result in congenital malformations in up to 10% of cases and a well-known valproate syndrome in up to 40% of children exposed to it in utero. This condition is associated with developmental and cognitive difficulties. NICE recommends that valproate is not used in women of child-bearing age unless there is no other alternative.

questions.question_text: What score on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) is suggestive of caseness?
questions.explanation: A score of 12-13 or above on the EPDS is suggestive of caseness (probable depression) in the postnatal period.

questions.question_text: The individual discovers that she is pregnant and chooses to remain on the longacting injectable formulation of paliperidone during pregnancy given the benefit she has had from the medication. You are asked to perform a consultation on her shortly after she delivers. The postpartum clinical approach of this individual involves:

options.text: Immediate separation of mother from the infant
An automatic referral to the Department of Child and Family Services
An automatic admission to the inpatient psychiatric unit
A careful evaluation of the individual, including assessing for hallucinations and delusions, and for risk of harm to herself and to the infant.
Immediate discontinuation of paliperidone due to breastfeeding

correct_answer.text: A careful evaluation of the individual, including assessing for hallucinations and delusions, and for risk of harm to herself and to the infant.

questions.explanation: The evaluation of patients with schizophrenia in the postpartum setting should be thorough, and particular y BoARd REVIEw attention should be paid to the safety of the patient and to that of the newborn infant. Many patients with schizophrenia are safely discharged with followup in outpatient care. Some may require inpatient admission especially if the patient is demonstrating rapid deterioration, command hallucinations, delusions involving the baby, suicidal ideation, aggression, or risk of harm to the infant. Many women with schizophrenia are able to parent, and a diagnosis alone does not warrant a social services referral. The presence of poorly controlled symptoms, concerns regarding the baby’s safety, absence of a supportive partner or family, unstable housing status, and presence of mental health problems are predictors of social services supervision and possible custody loss. Paliperidone is excreted in breast milk. The risk of infant exposure to paliperidone is unknown, and monitoring for extrapyramidal side effects in the baby is recommended. However, this would not be an indication to abruptly discontinue the medication.

questions.explanation: Combined use of carbamazepine and phenytoin during pregnancy is associated with finger nail hypoplasia as part of fetal anticonvulsant syndrome, along with other features such as facial dysmorphism and developmental delay.

questions.question_text: A 28-year-old woman develops acute confusion, mood lability, and persecutory delusions 5 days after giving birth to her first child. She has no previous psychiatric history. Which symptom domain is most common in postpartum psychosis?
questions.explanation: Affective symptoms (mood lability, depression, elation) are most common in postpartum psychosis.

questions.question_text: Which one is a screening tool for depression?
questions.explanation: The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) is a screening tool, while instruments like Hamilton and Montgomery-Åsberg are rating scales used for symptom severity assessment.

questions.question_text: Maternal smoking during pregnancy has been best linked to which of the following?

options.text: A diagnosis of autistic spectrum disorder

questions.explanation: Maternal smoking during pregnancy has been consistently associated with conduct disorder and delinquency and attention-defi cit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in offspring during childhood and adolescence. This association has been found even after controlling for confounding variables such as socioeconomic status, maternal age, birth weight, and maternal psychopathology. This may be due to the effect of nicotine or may be genetically mediated. There may be other environmental risks that play a part in its development. More recent research has shown that the behavioural problems may not be a direct risk of smoking itself, but the presence of other genetic factors that may mediate the association between maternal smoking and conduct problems in children. Button TM, Thapar A and McGuffi n P. Relationship between antisocial behaviour, attention-defi cit hyperactivity disorder and maternal prenatal smoking. British Journal of Psychiatry 2005; 187: 155–160.

questions.question_text: For the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS), what score suggests caseness for depression?
questions.explanation: A score of 12-13 or above on the EPDS is suggestive of caseness for postnatal depression.

questions.question_text: Postpartum Intrusive Thoughts A woman 1 year postpartum reports distressing intrusive thoughts of harming her baby. She finds these thoughts ego-dystonic and has no intention to act on them. She describes the birth as traumatic. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Ego-dystonic intrusive thoughts about harming the baby with no intent to act suggests postpartum OCD, not psychosis. The traumatic birth history could suggest PTSD, but intrusive harm thoughts are more characteristic of OCD.

questions.question_text: Ebstein anomaly is caused by maternal use of which medication?
questions.explanation: Ebstein anomaly, a congenital cardiac defect, is associated with maternal exposure to lithium during pregnancy, particularly in the first trimester.

questions.question_text: A jittery child with overarousal presents 2 hours after delivery. Which maternal substance is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Cocaine and heroin exposure in utero causes neonatal withdrawal syndrome characterized by jitteriness, overarousal, and hyperexcitability within hours of delivery.

questions.question_text: Which consequence of maternal depression is most likely to appear across ALL developmental stages?
questions.explanation: Affective consequences appear as anger/protective coping in infants, passive compliance in toddlers, affective disorders in school-age children, and depression/affective disorders in adolescents, making this the most consistent across development.

questions.question_text: A 34yearold female patient gives birth to a child who has short palpebral fissures, a smooth philtrum, and microcephaly. Based on the child’s physical appearance, which one of the following substances is this female patient most likely to have abused during pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Fetal alcohol syndrome affects about one third of all infants born to alcoholic women. It is characterized by growth retardation, microphthalmia, short palpebral fissures, midface hypoplasia (smooth or short philtrum and a thin upper lip), microcephaly, intellectual deficits, and seizures. The incidence of infants born with fetal alcohol syndrome is about 0.5 per 1,000 live births. Marijuana use in pregnancy is associated with low birth weight, prematurity, and withdrawal symptoms, including excessive crying, tremors, and hyperemesis. Crack cocaine use by the mother causes increased irritability and crying spells in infants. Heroin leads to withdrawal syndrome in infants. Nicotine causes low birth weight and premature births. hROUGh thE LIFE CYCLE • 91

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a fetal malformation associated with sodium valproate exposure?

questions.question_text: A 34yearold female patient gives birth to a child who has short palpebral fissures, a smooth philtrum, and microcephaly. Based on the child’s physical appearance, which one of the following substances is this female patient most likely to have abused during pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Fetal alcohol syndrome affects about one third of all infants born to alcoholic women. It is characterized by growth retardation, microphthalmia, short palpebral fissures, midface hypoplasia (smooth or short philtrum and a thin upper lip), microcephaly, intellectual deficits, and seizures. The incidence of infants born with fetal alcohol syndrome is about 0.5 per 1,000 live births. Marijuana use in pregnancy is associated with low birth weight, prematurity, and withdrawal symptoms, including excessive crying, tremors, and hyperemesis. Crack cocaine use by the mother causes increased irritability and crying spells in infants. Heroin leads to withdrawal syndrome in infants. Nicotine causes low birth weight and premature births. hROUGh thE LIFE CYCLE • 91

questions.question_text: A 25yearold female, G2P2, who is 10 days postpartum comes to the emergency room with severe leftsided headache with blurred vision. While in the emergency room, she has a general tonic–c lonic seizure. Initial head CT scan shows no acute findings, but MR venogram shows absent flow in the right transverse sinus, sigmoid sinus, and internal jugular vein. What is the appropriate treatment for this condition? t OF NEUROLOGICAL DISORDERS • 167
questions.explanation: Cerebral venous thrombosis is frequently missed and misdiagnosed because it is considered to be a rare clinical entity. It has been associated with hypercoagulable states as in pregnancy or postpartum or with the use of oral contraceptives. Although variable in presentation, it commonly presents with severe headaches, delirium, and seizures. Laboratory tests, including coagulation labs, can be useful, but definite diagnosis requires neuroimaging. Head CT scan can be normal in up to 30% of cases. MRI in conjunction with MR venography is highly sensitive and specific for this diagnosis. Treatment includes use of anticoagulants based on current guidelines. Mannitol can be useful for the management of intracranial pressure as needed. Valproate can be used for seizure prophylaxis.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which is least likely to be a presenting physical feature of a child with foetal alcohol syndrome (FAS)?
questions.explanation: Children with FAS commonly present with microcephaly rather than macrocephaly. It is well documented that alcohol and its metabolite acetaldehyde can have serious effects on the developing foetus. Currently, the estimated incidence of FAS is between 1 and 3 cases per 1000 live births. It is one of the most frequent causes of birth defects associated with learning disability, and the most common of non-hereditary causes of birth defects. Clinical features of FAS include prenatal and postnatal growth retardation, central nervous system abnormalities, usually with learning disability (up to severe), a characteristic facial dysmorphism (e.g., absent philtrum, fl attened nasal bridge, short palpebral fi ssures, epicanthic folds, and maxillary hypoplasia), and an array of other birth defects such as microcephaly, altered palmar creases, short stature, syndactyly, atrial septal defect and other heart abnormalities. Full-blown foetal alcohol syndrome is seen in the offspring of approximately one-third of alcoholic women drinking the equivalent of 10–15 units daily. It is also more common in women who binge drink. Lowinson JH, Ruiz P, Millman RB and Langrod JG. Substance Abuse: A Comprehensive Textbook, 4th edn. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2005, p. 1052.

questions.explanation: The evidence here is limited and sometimes confl icting. questions.question_text: Among the following, which is the best screening tool used in post-natal depression?

options.text: A diagnosis of edinburgh postnatal depression scale
A diagnosis of beck’s depression inventory

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of edinburgh postnatal depression scale

questions.explanation: Common somatic complaints of pregnancy may be misconstrued as symptoms of depression when using traditional depression assessment scales (such as the Beck Depression Inventory, the Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression, or the Center for Epidemiological Studies Depression Scale), symptoms of depression reported by pregnant women may be misidentifi ed as normal pregnancy-related complaints by treating obstetricians. Use of the 10-item Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale has been found to accurately identify depression in pregnant and postpartum women. This brief screening instrument has been validated in pregnant and postpartum populations and is easily incorporated for standard practice use in obstetrical treatment settings. Kaplan HI. questions.question_text: What is the most common co-occurring psychiatric diagnosis among individuals with significant prenatal alcohol exposure (fetal alcohol spectrum disorder)?
questions.explanation:
Mental health problems are identified in more than 90% of individuals with histories of significant prenatal alcohol exposure, and the single most common co-occurring diagnosis is attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. 

Environmental Risk Factor: Prenatal exposure to alcohol is explicitly identified as an important environmental risk factor contributing to the development of ADHD and related neurodevelopmental disruptions
.
Core Neurocognitive Profile: Individuals with FASD consistently exhibit neurocognitive and behavioral deficits that overlap with ADHD, including impulsivity, hyperactivity, poor impulse control, concrete thinking, memory deficits, and visuospatial problems
.
Associated Neurodevelopmental Conditions: FASD is also frequently accompanied by mild learning disability (intellectual disability) as well as speech and language difficultie

questions.explanation: Sodium valproate in pregnancy causes multiple congenital malformations in 8-12% of exposed fetuses, including facial dysmorphism, cleft lip and palate, craniostenosis, cardiac defects, renal and urogenital defects, and limb defects (including bilateral aplasia of the radius). questions.question_text: Maternal smoking during pregnancy has been best linked to which of the following?

options.text: A diagnosis of autistic spectrum disorder

questions.explanation: Maternal smoking during pregnancy has been consistently associated with conduct disorder and delinquency and attention-defi cit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in offspring during childhood and adolescence. This association has been found even after controlling for confounding variables such as socioeconomic status, maternal age, birth weight, and maternal psychopathology. This may be due to the effect of nicotine or may be genetically mediated. There may be other environmental risks that play a part in its development. More recent research has shown that the behavioural problems may not be a direct risk of smoking itself, but the presence of other genetic factors that may mediate the association between maternal smoking and conduct problems in children. questions.question_text: Among the following options, which is accurate regarding the risk of SSRIs in pregnancy?

options.text: SSRIs carry significant teratogenic risk in the first trimester.
SSRIs should be discontinued by the second trimester to reduce perinatal complications.
SNRIs have consistently lower risk than SSRIs in pregnancy
Risks and benefits of SSRIs for both mother and baby must be weighed against the potential risks of untreated depression during pregnancy.
All SSRIs are contraindicated in pregnancy regardless of trimester.

correct_answer.text: Risks and benefits of SSRIs for both mother and baby must be weighed against the potential risks of untreated depression during pregnancy.

questions.explanation: Data on the safety of antidepressants in pregnancy are mixed, but paroxetine in particular appears to have a greater risk of teratogenicity than other SSRIs. It is the only SSRI to have a category D pregnancy status; other SSRIs are category C. SSRIs may increase risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn. Untreated depression during pregnancy also increases risk of adverse outcomes for both mother and child, and balancing of risks and benefits of treatment versus no treatment should be conducted on a casebycase basis. Psychotherapy, electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), and light therapy pose no known teratogenic risk in pregnancy.

questions.question_text: Mrs Yanica Presley is a 32-year-old woman with a previous diagnosis of bipolar affective disorder and has had several previous episodes of mania requiring admission. She has responded well to Lithium and has had no relapses since it was started 3 years ago. She is currently 36 weeks pregnant and has been taking Lithium 600mg throughout her pregnancy. She is currently well in her mood and is not planning on breastfeeding. Which of the following would be the most appropriate action?

options.text: Do nothing and review after 1 week after delivery
Reduce dose to 400 mg, then repeat blood levels after 1 week
Continue lithium and check levels weekly until delivery and for 2 weeks after

correct_answer.text: Continue lithium and check levels weekly until delivery and for 2 weeks after

questions.explanation: Lithium can be continued throughout pregnancy provided adequate monitoring is provided. This typically involves 4-weekly monitoring until 34 weeks, then weekly until 2 weeks post-partum, with doses modified as appropriate. An increase in dose is often required in early pregnancy, with some reversal in late pregnancy. Women at high risk of relapse should not be left without effective treatment, making continuation of lithium appropriate for this well-controlled patient.

questions.question_text: Which statement most accurately characterizes postpartum hypomania?

options.text: It characteristically emerges during the third trimester of pregnancy.
It occurs in approximately 5-10% of postpartum women.
It is a risk factor for postpartum depression.
It is indistinguishable from normal maternal mood fluctuations in most cases.
It is more common in nulliparous women.

correct_answer.text: It is a risk factor for postpartum depression.

questions.explanation: Childbirth may be a specific trigger for a hypomanic episode, which can occur in 10%–20% of females in nonclinical populations and most typically in the early postpartum period. Distinguishing hypomania from the elated mood and reduced sleep that normally accompany the birth of a child may be challenging. Postpartum hypomania may foreshadow the onset of a depression that occurs in about half of females who experience postpartum “highs.” Accurate detection of bipolar II disorder may help in establishing appropriate treatment of the depression, which may reduce the risk of suicide and infanticide.

questions.explanation: Besides the increased risk of neural tube defects, valproate use in pregnancy is associated with lower IQs in children exposed to the medication in utero. Studies have revealed an inverse correlation between higher doses of maternal valproate and lower IQ in exposed offspring. The growing evidence showing correlations between maternal valproate use and higher rates of intellectual disability in exposed offspring indicates that valproate should not be used in pregnancy as a firstline agent in bipolar patients.

questions.question_text: According to DSM-5 criteria for premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), which of the following belongs to the group of core mood symptoms, at least one of which must be present to meet the diagnostic criteria?

options.text: Marked increase in energy and goal-directed behaviour
Changes in sleep pattern (insomnia or hypersomnia)

questions.explanation: DSM-5 Criterion B for PMDD requires that at least one of four core mood symptoms be present: marked affective lability, marked irritability or anger, marked depressed mood, or marked anxiety/tension. Marked affective lability (Option A) correctly belongs to this compulsory core group. Option B is factually wrong as PMDD involves decreased, not increased, interest in activities. Option C incorrectly restricts the sleep criterion to insomnia only, whereas DSM-5 allows either insomnia or hypersomnia. Option D (appetite change) is a supplementary Criterion C symptom, not a core requirement. Option E introduces a non-existent qualifier (\'nonrepetitive tasks\') absent from DSM-5.

questions.question_text: Floppy baby syndrome is a recognised complication associated with the use of which of the following psychotropic drugs in pregnancy?

questions.question_text: Which class of antidepressants, when used during pregnancy increases the risk of cleft lip/cleft palate in the new born?
questions.explanation: Existing research evidence has shown a connection between prenatal use of SSRI anti-depressants and the subsequent formation of birth defects like cleft lip and palate. In 2006, a Danish population-based cohort study published in Epidemiology reported that women taking SSRI antidepressants from 30 days before conception to the end of the first trimester were more likely to give birth to babies with congenital formations, which may include cleft lip and palate.

questions.question_text: Which of these drugs is likely to cause tricuspid valve displacement towards the apex of the right ventricle in the newborn, when used during pregnancy?

Lithium use has a well-known association with this cardiac malformation (relative risk is 10-20 times more than control). Some case reports have also implicated benzodiazepines, although this is rare.

questions.question_text: Women with mental health conditions often need to continue medication during pregnancy and breastfeeding. The benefit from medicines during this time must be balanced against possible risks to the newborn and neonate. Which of the following drugs is considered to be the most teratogenic?
questions.explanation: Sodium valproate is contra-indicated in women of child-bearing age unless it is absolutely necessary and other agents are ineffective. It is associated with a 10% risk of foetal malformations and a 40% of long-term cognitive difficulties in children exposed to it during gestation. Carbamazepine is also associated with an increased risk, but not to the same extent. Lithium is associated with an increase in risk, particularly for Epstein's anomaly. However, this finding has not been replicated in more recent studies and the absolute risk would be low based upon the original research (around ).
